title: Geometry and measurement bases
outcome: Distinguish equal-Z-probability states using another basis.
scope_note: Open to everyone. Review the quick recall if an idea is unfamiliar. Practice completion and understanding evidence are separate.
notation_contract: Operations run left to right. Qubit 0 is the least significant bit: |q1 q0⟩. Probabilities are exact model predictions; counts are samples.
recap: A complex coefficient; probability is its squared magnitude.
H maps 0 to plus and 1 to minus; H twice returns the input.
A basis determines the question; shots repeat preparation.
A phase difference can affect a later interference experiment.
A common phase leaves all physical predictions unchanged.

topics.title: Complex numbers and phase angles
topics.objective: An amplitude a+ib has squared magnitude a²+b².
learning_objectives: Explain why an imaginary amplitude still gives a real, nonnegative probability. Then multiply both amplitudes by i: what changes physically?
topics.teach_markdown: An amplitude a+ib has squared magnitude a²+b². The imaginary unit satisfies i²=−1, but a probability uses the squared magnitude, never the square of i alone. A phase rotates the amplitude arrow without changing its length. A common phase rotates the whole state without changing any measurement statistics; relative phase can change interference.

topics.title: Vectors, matrices, and operation order
topics.objective: A state is a column vector.
learning_objectives: Explain why identical Z probabilities do not make X→H and H→X equivalent. Name a measurement that distinguishes their outputs.
topics.teach_markdown: A state is a column vector. X swaps its entries; Z changes the sign of the second entry; H maps (a,b) to ((a+b)/√2,(a−b)/√2). Applying X then H means HX|ψ⟩ because the rightmost matrix acts first. Gates need not commute. Starting at |0⟩, X then H gives |−⟩ while H then X gives |+⟩. Both have equal Z probabilities, so inspect phase or measure in X.

topics.title: The Bloch sphere
topics.objective: A pure qubit can be written cos(θ/2)|0⟩ + e^(iφ)sin(θ/2)|1⟩.
learning_objectives: A qubit lies on the equator. Predict its Z probabilities and explain why its longitude still matters.
topics.teach_markdown: A pure qubit can be written cos(θ/2)|0⟩ + e^(iφ)sin(θ/2)|1⟩. Its Bloch coordinates are (sinθ cosφ, sinθ sinφ, cosθ). |0⟩ is north, |1⟩ south; |+⟩ lies on +x and |+i⟩ on +y. This sphere represents a state mathematically, not an electron orbit. Global phase has no separate point. Mixed states lie inside the sphere.

topics.title: Rotations and phase gates
learning_objectives: At which step can the Z chart first change with φ, and why? Predict the final result for φ=π.
topics.teach_markdown: P(φ)=diag(1,e^(iφ)) changes relative phase. Rz(φ)=diag(e^(−iφ/2),e^(iφ/2)) differs from P only by a global phase for this single-qubit comparison. H→P(φ)→H converts phase into a Z distribution: P0=cos²(φ/2), P1=sin²(φ/2). Ry rotates through real superpositions. A diagram transition is not a measured trajectory.

topics.title: X, Y, and Z measurement bases
topics.objective: Measurement asks a question in a chosen basis.
learning_objectives: Predict Y outcomes for |+i⟩, then explain how to read Y using a Z measurement device.
topics.teach_markdown: Measurement asks a question in a chosen basis. X has eigenstates |+⟩ and |−⟩; Y has (|0⟩±i|1⟩)/√2. To implement X readout using Z measurement, apply H first. For Y, execute S† then H. The returned 0/1 labels mean the +1/−1 eigenvalues of the chosen observable. Readout rotates the state; distinguish its final physical state from the original-basis projected state.

topics.title: State versus distribution challenge
topics.objective: A single histogram does not identify a quantum state.
learning_objectives: Give two states with the same Z chart and design a new measurement to distinguish them. Predict that measurement for both.
topics.teach_markdown: A single histogram does not identify a quantum state. |+⟩, |−⟩ and |+i⟩ have the same Z probabilities. X distinguishes plus and minus; Y reveals the imaginary relative phase. Repeated preparations let us estimate x=P_X(+)-P_X(−), and similarly y and z. Finite samples have uncertainty; a single shot cannot determine an arbitrary unknown state.
